title: Rachel Apa's Family Obituary: 'She Always Found Her Way to the Finish Line'
excerpt: The family of the 24-year-old who collapsed at Mile 24 of the New York City Marathon on November 1 remembered a former Bucknell field hockey player who ran her first marathon for the Parkinson's Foundation — and has founded the Rachel Apa Foundation to teach athletes about rhabdomyolysis.
body:
• Rachel Apa, 24, collapsed at Mile 24 of the New York City Marathon in Central Park on November 1, 2026 and died hours later; her family says doctors attributed her death to rhabdomyolysis, a breakdown of muscle tissue.
  • Her family's obituary describes her as "strong-willed and naturally took charge" and says she "always found her way to the finish line."
  • Apa, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, had just moved to Charleston, South Carolina, worked as a product manager at TE Connectivity and was pursuing an MBA at Charleston Southern University.
  • To help: her family has created the Rachel Apa Foundation to raise awareness of rhabdomyolysis. The family's GoFundMe, organised by Dominic Apa toward a $150,000 goal, had raised over $118,000 by November 7, according to the New York Post.

The family of Rachel Apa, the 24-year-old runner who collapsed in the home stretch of the New York City Marathon, has released her obituary, remembering her as someone who was "strong-willed and naturally took charge." Apa died hours after falling at Mile 24 of the race in Central Park on November 1, from the rare muscular condition rhabdomyolysis, according to the New York Post.

"With determination, discipline, and a heart fully committed to whatever she pursued, she always found her way to the finish line."

— Rachel Apa's family, in her obituary

A life in 24 years

"On Sunday, November 1, 2026, after running 24 miles at an incredible pace and with a grin that stretched ear to ear, the only thing strong enough to physically stop her body met Rachel on 85th Street," the family wrote. "Her spirit was so powerful and full of vitality that not even her body could contain it." Apa, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was a gifted athlete who loved animals, especially her dogs, whom her family described as "her forever children." She was also a brilliant baker: "She created a cookie recipe so perfect it had to be thrown away for the sake of our health," the obituary reads.

Apa had just moved to Charleston, South Carolina, where she worked as a product manager at electric connector manufacturing company TE Connectivity while pursuing her MBA at Charleston Southern University. "While most of us are defined by our goals and achievements, it would be considerably more accurate to say that Rachel defined everything she did," her family wrote. "Her drive came from many places, but her family and her faith were always at the center."

Why she was running

Apa was a former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University, and the marathon was her first. Before her death, she wrote on LinkedIn that she was running to raise money for the Parkinson's Foundation, after the disease killed her grandfather. She thanked him for teaching her to "stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges." Her father, Steve Apa, told the New York Times she had been in "perfect health" before the marathon; bystanders and physicians administered CPR at Mile 24, marathon medical staff used a defibrillator, and doctors at Mount Sinai Medical Center spent more than six hours trying to save her before she was declared dead at around 9:40 p.m., the Post reported in its earlier coverage.

The foundation in her name

Apa's family has created the Rachel Apa Foundation in her memory to raise awareness of the condition that caused her death. Readers who want to help can support the family's GoFundMe, "Support The Rachel Apa Foundation", organised by Dominic Apa: the family says all donations will create and fund the foundation, which is in the process of incorporating as a nonprofit, will educate athletes about rhabdomyolysis, and hopes in the longer term to advocate for rapid on-course medical care at endurance events. The campaign's goal is $150,000, and it had raised over $118,000 by November 7, according to the Post.
